feedback: When runoff carries a pollutant to sea, highlight that none of this happened at the sea itself — it began inland.
When the tally reaches roughly 80/20, note that about four-fifths of marine pollution comes from land, not ships (an approximate global estimate).
When overfishing is triggered, show the knock-on effect on other species, not just fewer of one fish.
If the learner expects ships to dominate, point to the growing land share and the river/drain pathway they just watched.
activities.intendedInsight: Most ocean POLLUTION (about four-fifths) starts on LAND, often far from any ship, and travels via drains, runoff and rivers to the sea. Ocean harms, including pollution and overfishing (which happens at sea from fishing boats), can then cascade through the marine food web rather than staying at one spot.
learnerActions: Look at a scene split between an inland town-and-farm on top and the ocean below.
Perform ordinary land actions: spread fertiliser on a field, drop a bottle by the kerb, flush the drains.
Trigger the rain and watch each pollutant wash into a stream, down a river, and out to sea.
Observe the consequences: the fertiliser feeds an algal bloom, and the bottle drifts out to sea and slowly breaks into fragments that a seabird or fish swallows, mistaking them for food.
Overfish a fish stock and watch the loss ripple visibly through a food-web overlay to other species.
Read a running source tally that shows land vs ship contributions, with land arriving at roughly four-fifths of the total.
activities.title: Live a day on land, then watch it reach the sea

feedback: If only visible litter and spills are named, prompt that an invisible gas (CO2) dissolving into seawater also counts as pollution because it makes water more acidic and attacks shells and coral.
If the learner thinks plastic breaks down and disappears, note that it persists and fragments into microplastics that animals eat.
Confirm correct harm→animal matches with the specific mechanism (e.g. the turtle mistook the bag for a jellyfish).
activities.intendedInsight: Each ocean harm has a concrete, nameable effect on real animals; plastic persists and fragments into microplastics, and CO2 is an invisible gas that still pollutes the water.
learnerActions: Match each harm to a specific animal and effect: plastic bag → turtle that eats it mistaking it for a jellyfish; plastic fragments → seabird with a stomach full of plastic; oil spill → otter with coated fur; overfishing → fewer fish left for seals and seabirds that eat them, disrupting the food web; CO2 → more acidic water that makes it harder for shellfish and coral to build and keep their shells and skeletons.
Name at least three distinct ways humans harm the ocean.
For one harm, state out loud or in writing exactly how it hurts a named animal.
activities.title: Harm–animal cards: naming harms through their victims

feedback: If the learner says banning ships would clean the ocean, point out that around 80% starts on land via litter, runoff, sewage and chemicals, so most of the problem would remain.
If the learner says plastic only harms the one turtle that swallows it, follow microplastics or a toxin up the web to show one input reaching many victims.
Distinguish a single dramatic oil spill (point source, rarer) from diffuse everyday runoff (nonpoint source, the larger cumulative problem).
activities.intendedInsight: Pollution does not stay where it enters: it spreads through currents and bioaccumulation up the food web, and because the bulk comes from land, stopping ship leaks alone would leave most of the problem untouched.
learnerActions: Trace a plastic bottle dropped on a city street hundreds of miles from the coast to the sea, naming the route (drain → river → sea).
Follow a toxin or microplastic from plankton up through fish to predators, noting that one input can reach many animals that never touched the plastic directly.
Explain whether banning all ships would mostly stop ocean pollution, and why or why not.
Explain how carbon dioxide, a gas in the air, can count as ocean pollution.
activities.title: One bottle, many victims: tracing a cascade

feedback: Probe the learner's reasoning rather than simply confirming: ask them to say how the bottle actually travels or how the collapse spreads.
Pair the problem with solutions so the framing is empowering rather than guilt- or doom-laden.
Redirect to the land-to-sea mechanism if the dialogue drifts to ships as the main cause.
activities.intendedInsight: Ocean harm has a values and agency dimension — who is responsible, whether distant inland behaviour matters, and what we can do — alongside the factual mechanism.
learnerActions: Ask a marine-biologist character 'how does MY town's rubbish reach the sea?' and respond to their follow-up questions about the runoff pathway.
Discuss why overfishing hurts more than just one fish, explaining the web disruption in your own words.
Hear a turtle character recount mistaking a plastic bag for a jellyfish, and discuss what could be done differently.
activities.title: Talking it through with a marine biologist or a sea turtle

feedback: For the source item, reinforce that about four-fifths is land-based via runoff, litter, sewage and chemicals.
For the scenario, confirm the full chain (land activity → river/drain → sea → effect on an animal → spread through the web).
Recognition items check whether the idea is held; they do not by themselves show the learner can independently construct and explain the pathway, so pair with the explain/trace tasks above.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can demonstrate naming harms, identifying the land-based majority source, and tracing a land activity to a cascading marine effect.
learnerActions: Name three ways humans harm the ocean.
Answer where most ocean pollution comes from — land or ships — and give the approximate share.
Work a scenario that traces a specific land activity through runoff to a cascading effect in the ocean food web.
activities.title: Check: pollution sources, main cause, and a traced cascade
